analysis.evidence: יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים is the speaker, and אֶל הַנָּחָשׁ identifies the serpent as the addressee. The direct speech begins with כִּי עָשִׂיתָ זֹּאת, “because you did this.”
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים אֶל הַנָּחָשׁ, יַהְוֶה names the speaker who addresses the serpent. אֱלֹהִים stands in apposition to the name.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Personal name of the God of Israel

analysis.evidence: אֱלֹהִים stands in apposition to יַהְוֶה. The singular verb וַיֹּאמֶר identifies יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים as the one speaker addressing the serpent.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute common noun with singular reference.

analysis.evidence: After וַיֹּאמֶר ‘said’, אֶל introduces הַנָּחָשׁ ‘the serpent’ as the addressee. The second-person pronoun אַתָּה ‘you’ confirms the direct address.
analysis.morphology: Preposition without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אֶל הַנָּחָשׁ identifies the serpent as the one Yahweh God addresses. The words עַל גְּחֹנְךָ תֵלֵךְ, “you will go on your belly,” describe its movement.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute common noun with the prefixed definite article הַ־.

analysis.evidence: כִּי עָשִׂיתָ זֹּאת (“because you have done this”) gives the reason for the verdict אָרוּר אַתָּה (“cursed are you”).
analysis.morphology: Uninflected causal conjunction with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: God addresses the serpent. In כִּי עָשִׂיתָ זֹּאת, “because you have done this,” זֹּאת is the direct object and points back to the serpent’s conduct as the reason for the curse.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, second person masculine singular

draft.change: Add a Hebrew root article for ארר with the Qal verb אָרַר and its passive participle אָרוּר.
draft.definition: To pronounce a curse on someone. The passive participle describes the one under the curse.
draft.evidence: In Gen.3.14 Yahweh pronounces the serpent cursed for what it has done and declares how it will live.

analysis.evidence: In אָרוּר אַתָּה, “cursed are you,” the participle agrees with אַתָּה, the serpent Yahweh addresses. כִּי עָשִׂיתָ זֹּאת gives the reason for the curse, and the rest of the verse states its consequences: the serpent will go on its belly and eat dust all its life.
analysis.morphology: Qal passive participle, masculine singular absolute, used predicatively without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: To pronounce a curse on someone.

analysis.evidence: אֶל הַנָּחָשׁ identifies the serpent as the addressee. In אָרוּר אַתָּה, “cursed are you,” אַתָּה is the subject and אָרוּר states what is true of the serpent.
analysis.morphology: Independent second-person masculine singular pronoun, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: you (are): the one addressed named or identified

analysis.evidence: In אָרוּר אַתָּה מִכָּל הַבְּהֵמָה, כֹּל modifies the collective noun הַבְּהֵמָה. The serpent is cursed more than all the livestock.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with prefixed comparative מִן. The נ assimilates to the following כ.

analysis.evidence: The serpent is cursed more than both הַבְּהֵמָה and חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה, “the wild animals of the field.” The pairing identifies הַבְּהֵמָה as livestock collectively.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ + feminine singular absolute common noun, used collectively.

analysis.evidence: חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה denotes the wild animals collectively. כֹּל includes that entire group in the comparison with the serpent, parallel to מִכָּל הַבְּהֵמָה in the preceding phrase.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state, prefixed with the conjunction וּ־ and the comparative preposition מִן, whose נ assimilates to כ.

analysis.evidence: חַיַּת takes הַשָּׂדֶה as its complement. The phrase וּמִכֹּל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה means “and more than every wild animal of the field,” pairing the wild animals with the livestock in מִכָּל הַבְּהֵמָה.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular noun in the construct state, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: wild beast, beast of the field

analysis.evidence: In חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה, “animal of the open country,” הַשָּׂדֶה names the animal’s habitat. The contrast with הַבְּהֵמָה, “the livestock,” supports this reading.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun.
analysis.sense: open country, the land outside town and house

analysis.evidence: In עַל גְּחֹנְךָ תֵלֵךְ, “you will go on your belly,” עַל introduces the body part on which the serpent will move.
analysis.morphology: Preposition without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add a Hebrew noun entry for גָּחוֹן with the anatomical sense “belly.”
draft.definition: The belly or underside on which an animal crawls.
draft.evidence: Genesis 3:14 names the serpent’s belly as the part on which it will go. Leviticus 11:42 uses the same expression to distinguish animals that move on the belly from those that walk on four feet or have many feet.

analysis.evidence: Yahweh tells the serpent עַל גְּחֹנְךָ תֵלֵךְ, “on your belly you shall go.” The preposition עַל and the verb תֵלֵךְ identify the belly as the part on which the serpent moves. The suffix ךָ refers to the serpent.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state with the second-person masculine singular possessive suffix ךָ.
analysis.sense: The belly or underside of a crawling animal.

analysis.evidence: God addresses the serpent directly. In עַל גְּחֹנְךָ תֵלֵךְ, “on your belly you shall go,” תֵלֵךְ expresses motion and עַל גְּחֹנְךָ specifies how the serpent will move.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, second person masculine singular, with preformative ת־ and no suffix.
analysis.sense: go, move from place to place

analysis.evidence: In וְעָפָר תֹּאכַל, “and dust you will eat,” עָפָר is the direct object of תֹּאכַל. The preceding words עַל גְּחֹנְךָ תֵלֵךְ, “you will go on your belly,” identify the dust as the loose earth at the serpent’s mouth. The image conveys humiliation within the curse.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וְ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun.

analysis.evidence: God addresses the serpent as אַתָּה. In וְעָפָר תֹּאכַל, עָפָר (“dust”) is the object of תֹּאכַל (“you will eat”).
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, second person masculine singular

analysis.evidence: In כָּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ, “all the days of your life,” כָּל takes the plural יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ as its complement. The phrase gives the duration of the serpent’s eating dust, extending it over its whole lifetime.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כָּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ, “all the days of your life,” יְמֵי takes חַיֶּיךָ, “your life,” as its complement. The phrase extends the curse throughout the serpent’s lifetime.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural noun in the construct state.
analysis.sense: (pl.) days of a life, a reign or an age

analysis.evidence: In כָּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ, “all the days of your life,” the suffix refers to the serpent. The phrase gives the duration of the curse as the serpent’s entire lifetime.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural noun in the construct state with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix.
analysis.sense: lifetime, the days of one's life
